title: Green member behind Zionism motion named as 'close friend' of jailed al-Qaeda supporter in court
description: The Green Party member behind a motion which declared Zionism to be racism was named in court documents as a "close friend" of a man who was jailed af
body: The Green Party member behind a motion which declared Zionism to be racism was named in court documents as a "close friend" of a man who was jailed after being accused of plotting a suicide bomb attack at Heathrow Airport.Lubna Speitan, a British-Palestinian artist, proposed the Green conference motion defining Zionism as an ideology supporting "an ethnonationalist Jewish state".Court documents from 2015 show she offered to testify as a defence witness in the trial of Minh Quang Pham, who was jailed for 40 years in the US after pleading guilty to supporting al-Qaeda. He denied planning a suicide attack.The BBC has contacted Speitan for comment. The Green Party said she holds no official positions and the party "takes all allegations of this nature seriously".The motion proposed by Speitan, which was passed on Sunday to become party policy, called for a "single democratic Palestinian state in all of historic Palestine", which includes modern-day Israel.In response, Israel banned Green leader Zack Polanski from entering the country, while Jewish groups described it as an "attack" on their community and some Labour and Lib Dem MPs reported the party to Great Britain's equality watchdog.Speitan argued its backers wanted to voice opposition to "racist systems of oppression".On Tuesday, it emerged she wrote a letter in 2016 to the New York judge in the Pham case describing him as "one of the kindest, honest, most sincere" people she had known. The existence of the letter was first reported by the Jewish Chronicle, external and it has been seen by BBC News.Pham, a Vietnamese-born British national who had lived in London, was arrested at Heathrow Airport in July 2011 after spending seven months in Yemen. He was found in possession of a live round of ammunition.In 2015 he was extradited to the US and in 2016 sentenced to 40 years in prison after he admitted three counts based on his support for the group al-Qaeda in the Arabian Peninsula (AQAP), an offshoot of al-Qaeda. US prosecutors said Pham was directed by al-Qaeda leader Anwar al-Awlaki to detonate explosives in Heathrow's arrivals area after spending several months in Yemen being trained by him. In US court documents from 2015, Speitan was listed as a "close friend" of Pham who would provide "critical testimony regarding Pham's mental state". The documents said that would be "crucial in establishing a mental health defense", adding that "bears on the issue of guilt".Speitan had a medical condition that prevented her from giving evidence in person, the documents add. In a later letter to the US District Judge, Speitan said Pham was one of the "few people I regard with such high respect and esteem".She said if the judge "truly knew the Minh [Pham] that and others grew to love and respect", they may have "probably had the whole case dismissed".She acknowledged he "may have had and developed some behavioural issues" but added: "He turned out to be one of the kindest, honest, most sincere, trustworthy and respectful people I have ever known."There is no suggestion in the documents that Speitan knew of Pham's criminal activities at the time they knew each other.Speitan has not responded to the BBC's request for comment. The Telegraph reported that when it asked her if she remained friends with Pham, she replied: "Yes, it's still the case."She was reported as saying she believed Pham had been "targeted" by "the system".A Green Party spokesperson said: "Where members have expressed views that do not fit in with the party's values, we have internal processes to investigate."It came as Green leader Polanski grappled with division among the party's members, MPs and deputy leaders over the motion. Some Green councillors have resigned since it was passed. Green deputy leader in Wales, Phil Davies, resigned and cancelled his membership on Tuesday, describing the motion as "the final nail in the coffin".Polanski released a lengthy statement on Monday night to say he would not accept anyone being excluded from the party "because of the religious or communal body they are part of".The party leader, who is Jewish, added that "antisemitism and criticism of the Israeli state are, and must always be, completely distinct".Additional reporting by Imogen Wallace

schema.headline: Green member behind Zionism motion named as 'close friend' of jailed al-Qaeda supporter in court

title: Man charged with Dersingham GP Dr Hannah Terry's murder
description: A man has been charged with the murder of a GP who was found dead at her home.The man was arrested after the body of 45-year-old Dr Hannah Terry, also
body: A man has been charged with the murder of a GP who was found dead at her home.The man was arrested after the body of 45-year-old Dr Hannah Terry, also known as Hannah Cain, was found at a property in Fern Hill, Dersingham, Norfolk, on Sunday.Norfolk Police said 45-year old Mark Cain, of Fern Hill, Dersingham, has been charged with her murder.He has been remanded in custody until a court appearance on Wednesday.A notice on the website of Grimston Medical Centre, where Dr Terry is listed as a member of the practice team, said it was "temporarily closed due to extremely difficult circumstances affecting our practice team".Tributes have been left outside the centre, including a teddy bear and flowers on a bench. A card from two patients reads: "Dear Dr Hannah Terry. We are so shocked and saddened to hear such tragic news."

schema.headline: Man charged with Dersingham GP Dr Hannah Terry's murder

title: PCs who used Taser and baton on Donald Burgess at care home sacked
description: During a week-long hearing, force lawyer Aaron Rathmell told the panel Smith, 52, and Comotto, 37, "acted, hastily, harshly and lost control".He said
body: During a week-long hearing, force lawyer Aaron Rathmell told the panel Smith, 52, and Comotto, 37, "acted, hastily, harshly and lost control".He said Smith had drawn the pepper spray within nine seconds of entering Burgess's room.Bodyworn camera footage showed Smith walking into the room and saying: "Do you want to be sprayed or Tasered? It's up to you. Can you put that down for us?"Despite repeated requests, Burgess, who was a single leg amputee, did not drop the dinner knife.The panel found Smith "made no attempt to assess or understand" Burgess' vulnerability, while Comotto "showed no compassion".The following video contains distressing scenes.Smith failed to consider leaving the 92-year-old in his room to calm down, the panel found, plus the use of Pava, a type of pepper spray, was deemed unreasonable in the circumstances.There was "limited mitigation" for this behaviour, it said.The panel also said Smith's tone and language towards Burgess was "dismissive in nature", while Comotto was "antagonistic".Comotto's statements - such as "last chance" or "seriously" - and giving Burgess limited time to respond, were found to be inappropriate. The panel found her use of force to be unreasonable.Comotto had previously told the hearing that other officers at Hastings police station "were laughing and joking at my expense for deploying a Taser in a care home".She also faced a separate allegation relating to comments posted following the incident.In birthday Facebook post which said the care home was "getting closer and closer", Comotto replied: "We all know what happens in care homes", followed by a lightning bolt emoji.During the hearing, Rathmell told Comotto: "You made light of the situation and the use of the Taser on an elderly and vulnerable resident in a care home. This was inappropriate and/or unprofessional."Assistant Chief Constable Peter Gardner said Burgess was in his own room, isolated from residents and posed no risk. More information should have been ascertained from care home staff, he said.Gardner added that Smith had shown a lack of remorse and insight into the inappropriateness of his actions, and the panel remained concerned by his evidence which stated he would not do anything differently.While noting Comotto's remorse and evidence that she would act differently, Gardner said the reputation of the police service, along with public confidence in it, must be upheld.After the hearing, Deputy Chief Constable Paul Court said he was "appalled" by the officers' actions and apologised to the Burgess family.He said Smith and Comotto's behaviour "in no way reflects the conduct of those who serve in Sussex Police, particularly when responding to incidents involving vulnerable people and those in crisis".He said police officers "can often find themselves in challenging and unpredictable situations, where they must make split-second decisions to keep the public safe and to do so with measure, compassion and skill."This was not one of those cases."Speaking after the hearing, Burgess' great nephew, Jason Pye, called him "a much loved family man" who should be "remembered for the life he lived and not simply for the events which brought us to this point".He said justice had been served and dismissal from Sussex Police was "the only outcome there could have been" for Smith and Comotto.He added: "I hope this is a warning to all officers who show that sort of behaviour going forward."Follow BBC Sussex on Facebook, external, on X, external, and on Instagram, external and listen to BBC Radio Sussex on Sounds. Send your story ideas to southeasttoday@bbc.co.uk, external or WhatsApp us on 08081 002250.

title: Roll-out begins for passport-free UK airport e-gates
description: Passengers arriving into the UK will be able to pass through airport e-gates without showing their passport under a new contactless system, the govern
body: Passengers arriving into the UK will be able to pass through airport e-gates without showing their passport under a new contactless system, the government has announced.On Tuesday, East Midlands Airport became the first airport to offer the new technology before it is rolled out to all UK airports by early 2027, the Home Office said.The system uses facial technology so as passengers approach the e-gate, their photo is taken and then checked against immigration, travel and passport information and, if verfied, the barrier opens automatically.Testing showed the new contactless system was up to 25% faster than using a passport, according to officials.If further checks are needed, travellers will need to put their passport on the reader or may be directed to a Border Force officer.Officers will continue to monitor all e-gates and offer assistance, while passengers should keep their passport with them at all times, the Home Office said.Phil Douglas, director general of Border Force, said: "This is a win for travellers coming to our brilliant country."By using state-of-the-art technology, we are making journeys smoother and faster, all while fully maintaining the UK's robust border security."Our digital transformation also builds on our work this summer to extend eGates to children aged eight and above, making life a little easier for families."Karen Dee, chief executive of Airports UK, the trade body for the country's airports, said the move was "excellent news for the passenger".She added: "It is vital that we have the fast, efficient borders that arrivals into the UK now expect, and we will work closely with our members and government officials to ensure a smooth rollout."Steve Griffiths, managing director of East Midlands Airport, in Castle Donington, Leicestershire, said: "We're delighted to be the first UK airport to have contactless e-gates introduced by Border Force."As an airport committed to providing an effortless travel experience, we welcome any technological innovation that can help to safely make our customers' journeys smoother, swifter and simpler."This complements changes that we carried out to our immigration hall recently to help improve the flow of arriving passengers through the area."Standard e-gates are currently available at Birmingham, Bristol, Cardiff, East Midlands, Edinburgh, Gatwick, Glasgow, Heathrow, London City, Luton, Manchester, Newcastle and Stansted.

schema.headline: Roll-out begins for passport-free UK airport e-gates

title: England: What has boss Thomas Tuchel learned during international break?
description: There was a sense of inevitability that England captain Kane would be the star turn in Tuesday's 3-0 win over the Czech Republic as he celebrated equa
body: There was a sense of inevitability that England captain Kane would be the star turn in Tuesday's 3-0 win over the Czech Republic as he celebrated equalling Peter Shilton's record of 125 England caps.Kane, still irreplaceable at 33, added to his goals tally as England's all-time record scorer, his total of 91 now 38 ahead of Wayne Rooney, who is in second place in the listings with 53 goals in 120 games.And, with Kane still looking in his prime and fully fit, it now seems only a matter of time before he makes history as the first player to score 100 goals for England.This alone will have delighted Tuchel, but even more satisfying for the German is that he now presides over an attacking quartet that can pose a threat to any side in world football.Kane is the peerless spearhead, but Anthony Gordon - on target in the three Nations League games against Spain, the Czech Republic and Croatia before being rested here at Wembley - has moved his game on to another level since joining Barcelona from Newcastle.Gordon is a creator with burning pace, while on the right flank Bukayo Saka has looked rejuvenated after a World Cup during which he was hampered by an Achilles injury, as he proved with two goals in Croatia.And, just behind them all, with everything he does stamped with world class, is Jude Bellingham, England's player of the year and the golden future of his country at only 23.This may be bad news for Chelsea's Cole Palmer, whose withdrawal from England's squad has allowed others to cement their place in front of him, with Nottingham Forest's Morgan Gibbs-White proving his commitment by cutting short a family holiday to join the squad after being excluded initially.England's front four looks a natural fit, augmented by Chelsea's Morgan Rogers, while Liverpool's 18-year-old Rio Ngumoha will be an international contender for years to come.If Tuchel can keep his fab four fit and firing, England will be a danger to any opponents.In a camp of positives, a major disappointment for England and Tuchel was the injury suffered by Bournemouth midfielder Alex Scott after an outstanding debut in the 7-0 win in Croatia.Scott slipped seamlessly into England's midfield with powerful running, a complete range of passing and an energy to his link play that made the 23-year-old look perfectly at home at international level.Scott's emergence showed the array of riches Tuchel has at his disposal in the central midfield area, even with Arsenal's Declan Rice, a fixture in the team, out as his load is managed after injury.Indeed, Scott was so impressive that Tuchel said: "Is Declan still for me a fixed point in my team? Yes, but some other players are coming and impressing and it's an ongoing competition."It was hardly a shot across Rice's bows, but certainly an indication of the options available to England.So the thigh injury that ruled him out against the Czech Republic was a blow to Scott and England - as well as Bournemouth, who fear he will be sidelined for two months.Elliot Anderson, Manchester City's £116m summer purchase from Nottingham Forest, also goes from strength to strength after a good World Cup, while Tuchel was prepared to give Arsenal's 20-year-old Myles Lewis-Skelly his head in central midfield in these Nations League games.Everton's James Garner has also figured and has a big admirer in Tuchel, even referring to him as England's "mini Valverde" - a somewhat tongue-in-cheek reference to Real Madrid midfielder Federico perhaps, but a sign of how highly he is rated.Manchester United's Kobbie Mainoo pulled out injured while Crystal Palace's Adam Wharton, so highly-rated, has been unable to force his way into Tuchel's plans.Tuchel's treatment of Trent Alexander-Arnold had provided a constant backdrop to his time as England head coach, with what appeared to be his mistrust of the Real Madrid right-back's defensive frailties culminating in his exclusion from the World Cup squad.Alexander-Arnold's card looked marked from the moment Tuchel, after leaving him out of World Cup qualifiers against Andorra and Serbia in August 2025, said: "If he wants to have this impact in the English national team then he has to take the defensive part very, very seriously."Because when we are talking, especially about qualifying football, and then tournament football, the one defensive error, the one moment where you are not 100% awake, can be decisive. It can be the moment where you pack your suitcases and go home."Tuchel, however, appeared to set those reservations to one side when he recalled him for these four Nations League games - and Alexander-Arnold responded with performances that simply demand his continued inclusion.The 27-year-old made his first start under Tuchel - in fact his first since scoring in the Nations League win in Finland in October 2024 - against the Czech Republic in Prague, demonstrating the extra dimension he offers England with a world-class cross for Gordon's opener.Alexander-Arnold was a potent force once more against the Czechs at Wembley, forcing a fine early save from keeper Lukas Hornicek with a 30-yard free-kick then providing several more trademark dangerous crosses.True, any potential defensive deficiencies were not probed, but Alexander-Arnold showed enough class and creation to surely avoid being discarded again by Tuchel.Newcastle United's Lewis Hall emerged as one of the big winners from England's opening round of Nations League matches, making a strong case to become Tuchel's long-term left-back.Hall stepped in for three matches after Manchester City's Nico O'Reilly, first choice at the World Cup and for the opening game against Spain, returned to his club with an injury.It allowed Hall, who has just signed a new contract tying him to Newcastle until 2031, the opportunity to stake his claim - and he did so in style.The 22-year-old impressed in both games against Czech Republic and also in the rout in Croatia, with one key factor sure to play out in his favour.Hall's left-flank partnership with former Newcastle United team-mate Gordon looked a natural fit, the pair working in tandem to perfection in a manner that will give Tuchel serious food for thought.O'Reilly has done nothing wrong, but questions remain as to whether he is a natural left-back or simply a converted midfield player.Hall looked the part in every respect. He has made it difficult for Tuchel to leave him out, the link with Gordon only adding to the attraction for England's head coach.

schema.headline: England: What has boss Thomas Tuchel learned during international break?

title: Paramount-Warner Bros merger: Four ways the deal could affect you
description: From films to streaming prices - how the Warner Bros deal could affect youFigure caption, Watch: What the Paramount and Warner Bros deal means for you
body: From films to streaming prices - how the Warner Bros deal could affect youFigure caption, Watch: What the Paramount and Warner Bros deal means for youByFrancisco VelasquezBusiness reporterReporting fromNew York and Regan MorrisReporting fromCaliforniaIt has been months in the making but Paramount Skydance has finally completed its $110bn (£82.8bn) merger with Warner Bros Discovery.The deal welds two legacy Hollywood powerhouses, uniting franchises like Harry Potter and Game of Thrones, into an entertainment behemoth named Skydance.Yet behind this milestone lies strict rules about what the combined business can and cannot do - from how many films it must produce a year to the editorial independence of its newsroom.  Here are four ways this could affect you and the movies, TV and news you watch.1. Streaming prices may riseImage source, Eddy Chen/HBOImage caption, HBO Max is the company behind Euphoria, a series starring ZendayaWarner Bros owns HBO Max, home to The Sopranos, House of the Dragon and Euphoria among others. Meanwhile, Paramount Skydance has Paramount+, which streams the likes of Yellowstone, Parks and Recreation and NCIS. Combining HBO Max and Paramount+ into a single platform or bundle will likely squeeze subscribers' wallets over time. While existing subscribers to both might enjoy short-term savings, analysts expect overall prices to rise as the combined giant seeks profitability.The merged company, Skydance, carries a massive $80bn in debt from the deal, even as executives target $6bn in annual cost savings.Analysts warn that consumers will ultimately bear the financial burden of the $110bn deal. Mike Proulx, research director at Forrester, noted that with streaming services constantly raising fees to increase profitability and Skydance saddled with massive debt, price increases are likely to come. While viewers will gain access to a broader catalog, as Skydance shifts toward a Paramount+ and HBO Max bundle rather than a single app, Proulx warns that "it's far-fetched to think it'll prevent downstream price hikes". 2. More film releasesImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Paramount and Warner Bros are coming together to form SkydanceAs part of a settlement deal with US states who had objected to the merger, Paramount Skydance has agreed to release a set number of films every year for the next five years. For the first two years, that's 30 movies annually, and for the remaining period it has to release 32 films each year.That's 156 movies in total - and the majority have to be "wide releases," meaning they must to be shown in cinemas. The merged studio must also release at least four independent films each year.If Skydance misses its movie quota, it could be forced to sell its 49% stake in Miramax – the studio co-founded by disgraced Hollywood mogul Harvey Weinstein. Breanne Gilliam, a corporate lawyer at Maddin Hauser, said the film commitment is meaningful, even if it comes with an expiration date."Once those obligations expire, the company will have far more flexibility," she said."Temporary rules cannot permanently fix a structural market shift".  Once the five-year deal ends, Skydance could follow rivals like Disney and Netflix by prioritizing streaming over cinema. As Disney's $71bn buyout of 21st Century Fox in 2019 proved, mega-deals can lead to fewer films in cinemas. Before the acquisition, 20th Century Fox routinely released 12 to 17 movies annually in theatres, but under Disney that slate scaled down to just three to six a year. 3. Hollywood jobs could be hitImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Members of the film and TV industry protested outside Paramount Studios in LAFor those working behind the scenes, the merger of two historic studios has been described as a "disaster" by those on the ground. Actors and writers recently gathered at Paramount Studios in Los Angeles to oppose the deal, accusing regulators of failing to protect industry livelihoods. Criminal Minds star Kirsten Vangsness told the BBC she was "heartbroken". "It's people that make this city," she said. "It's people that make entertainment,  it's the everyday creatives that this industry is built on - this is who it hurts."A report by consultancy CVL Economics for LA County estimated the merger could eliminate roughly 4,500 direct film and TV jobs, while causing $1.26bn in lost wages over three years. The blow could hit a region that has already lost roughly a third of its film and TV workforce, about 50,000 jobs, since 2022.Syleecia Thompson, a business professor at National University, said that "it hits small businesses, vendors, caterers and local communities". She warned that Hollywood may become less of a "single location" and more of a "dispersed network."Although the settlement establishes a workforce fund to retrain displaced workers, lawyers note it does not block job cuts. "Nothing in the settlement limits layoffs," attorney Gilliam added. 4. CNN and CBS could changeImage source, ReutersImage caption,  CNN White House correspondent Betsy Klein reports from outside the buildingTo address concerns over journalistic independence at CNN and CBS, the settlement creates a news editorial independence board that will be appointed directly by Paramount. The $110bn deal brings two major US television news operations under a single corporate roof. Before the deal, Paramount owned CBS News, and Warner Bros. owned CNN. Both networks have faced intense political pressure - CNN was one of a handful of news organisations banned from the White House by President Donald Trump - as well as leadership shifts amid broader industry consolidation. Paramount chief executive David Ellison has asked CNN boss Mark Thompson - the former director general of the BBC - to remain at the helm after the takeover closes. CBS News's editor-in-chief Bari Weiss will remain in her role. Yet as Paramount targets billions in cost cuts across the merged company, staff fear the consolidation will trigger significant job losses at CNN and CBS. Beyond potential workforce reductions, media advocates and legal experts remain deeply skeptical about whether it can ensure newsroom freedom.  Seth Stern, chief of advocacy at Freedom of the Press Foundation, described the Paramount-appointed board as "worthless"."The board creates the same First Amendment problems it claims to solve, the government meddling in news," Stern said. Gilliam agrees paper promises mean little without real authority. "An oversight board only has as much power as the agreement gives it. Oversight without authority is just observation," she said. schema.headline: Paramount-Warner Bros merger: Four ways the deal could affect you

title: Worcestershire student admits murdering woman in 'Dexter' kill room
description: Warning: This article contains details that readers may find distressingA forensic science student obsessed with the US television drama Dexter has ad
body: Warning: This article contains details that readers may find distressingA forensic science student obsessed with the US television drama Dexter has admitted murdering a 24-year-old woman after luring her to a plastic-lined "kill room" inside an Airbnb.Benjamin William Day, 20, changed his plea to guilty on the second day of his trial at Wolverhampton Crown Court.Prosecutors said he had carefully planned the killing of Maria Saceanu on 20 December, preparing a room with plastic sheeting and items intended to help him murder her and dispose of evidence.Day, who was 19 when the murder took place, was remanded in custody and is due to be sentenced on 4 December.The University of Worcester undergraduate, of Yeadon Close in Redditch, Worcestershire, had been expected to argue he acted in self-defence and had set up the room to film a Dexter tribute for TikTok.But after an hour-long delay to proceedings earlier, Day returned to the dock and appeared to smirk as he entered a guilty plea.Prosecutor Rachel Brand KC said he had been fascinated by the programme Dexter, which centres on a forensic scientist in a police department who knows how to cover his own tracks as a serial killer.Day had set up the the rented room in the Tividale area of the West Midlands to emulate the character - lining the walls and floor with plastic sheeting to cover his tracks and amassing a "shopping list" of items, including an apron, a plastic visor and cleaning chemicals. The first day of the trial heard that after causing 78 knife wounds to sex worker Saceanu, who he contacted through a website using a burner phone, Day abandoned the "gruesome task" of dismemberment because he cut himself.Prosecutors claim Day left the Airbnb after the killing, walked some distance away, and called 999 at 00:50 on 21 December asking for medical help.On body cam footage played to jurors on Tuesday, Day could be seen sitting in a police car with his hand wrapped in duct tape.He said he had been going to drink in Dudley and had been looking for a "random girl" in a bar when he claimed he had been injured near a bush by an animal that "might have been a fox". Questioned as to where he had got duct tape to wrap around his hand, Day told police it was in his car, although he could not remember where it was parked.A male officer told him that his story did not quite check out, to which Day responded: "I don't know if it was a wild dog or a fox."Police were alerted to the scene at the Airbnb by the property's landlord, who had been contacted by another resident who had booked into a different room and had discovered a trail of blood. In a statement the resident told jurors they had pushed open the door and saw "a lot of blood on the floor" and what appeared to be a doll. "The doll was lying on the floor on its back," they added. When Day was arrested on suspicion of murder at Russells Hall Hospital in Dudley in the early hours of the morning of 21 December he was wearing a khaki top resembling one worn by Dexter.A Home Office pathologist said Saceanu, originally from Romania, probably died as a result or wounds to her neck, causing damage to her carotid arteries, with a number of wounds to her hands "consistent with efforts to protect herself".Defence barrister Gurdeep Garcha KC said of Day: "He is well aware of the nature and inevitability of the sentence that must follow."It seems to us that given his age and the absence of (previous) criminal offending, the court would be assisted by a pre-sentence report."

schema.headline: Worcestershire student admits murdering woman in 'Dexter' kill room

title: Cristiano Ronaldo: Portugal forward not retiring but says he wants to be punished for walking out
description: Cristiano Ronaldo says he is not retiring from international football but deserves to be punished for walking out on Portugal after head coach Jorge J
body: Cristiano Ronaldo says he is not retiring from international football but deserves to be punished for walking out on Portugal after head coach Jorge Jesus twice "broke his word".The 41-year-old captain left his country's Nations League camp last week after being an unused substitute against Norway and then finding out he would not start against Denmark.Al-Nassr forward Ronaldo has scored 146 goals in 234 Portugal appearances - both world records - helping them win Euro 2016 and the Nations League twice.In a lengthy statement, external, which ran to nearly 2,000 words, the former Real Madrid and Manchester United player said he should be held accountable for his actions.But he accused Jesus of an "absolute breach of trust" for firstly not playing him against Norway after saying he would, before going back on a decision to present an agreed version of events to the media."The Portuguese Football Federation must assess the consequences of my actions and punish me for them. I believe the punishment should not be reduced," Ronaldo said."I have already apologised, but I know that actions have consequences."Ronaldo's statement comes after Portugal head coach Jesus said there was no rift with the captain, following claims the five-time Ballon d'Or winner had refused to train.Jesus said on Sunday that the door was still open for Ronaldo to play for the country's national team.Ronaldo said that, provided he was "physically fit, playing with my team, and hopefully scoring goals", he would like to continue to play international football."After my suspension period ends, I will be available, as I always have been, to compete and win with our national team," he added.BBC Sport has approached the Portuguese Football Federation (FPF) for comment.Ronaldo's statement struck a conciliatory tone in places, but he was also critical of Portugal coach Jesus as he provided his version of the dispute which prompted him to walk out on the squad last week.He said Jesus had agreed a plan under which the forward would miss the Norway and Denmark matches to manage his fitness.However, on the day of the Norway game, the 72-year-old coach told him he would play for 30 minutes."Everyone knows the rest. I warmed up from half-time onwards, watched the minutes tick by and wasn't called on," Ronaldo said."The manager had broken his word to me."A later meeting with Jesus produced an agreement for the coach to clarify matters at his next news conference.Ronaldo said an eight-point document was prepared saying he had never demanded playing time, had respected Jesus' decisions and that the coach asking "someone of the stature of Pele or Maradona" to warm up without bringing him on had been a mistake.Portugal's record appearance holder said the agreed notes did not require Jesus to apologise to him but said the coach's public remarks did not reflect their private discussion."The conference was what is known: the attitude had nothing to do with our meeting," Ronaldo explained. "I heard expressions and an aggressiveness I believe I did not deserve, a "High and mighty" attitude that he never showed me, not even remotely, in private the day before."Ronaldo said it was the "second time" Jesus had "broken his word to me" and he decided to leave the training camp "without waiting for any further broken promises".Prior to his appointment as head coach, Ronaldo said he had described Jesus - who had previously managed him at Al Nassr - as the "right choice".Ronaldo had considered retiring from international football after this summer's World Cup - at which Portugal exited at the last-16 stage - and said he had written a letter to fans containing the words he wanted to tell them when he announced it, but he was urged to reconsider by the FPF's president, Pedro Proenca, on the flight home from the United States.Ronaldo's behaviour drew contrasting opinions in his homeland with Jesus getting some support in the media and among fans at odds with those loyal to legendary player.Ronaldo said that, despite the "absolute breakdown of trust" in Jesus' word, he should not have left and the "responsibility is mine alone", as he said sorry to his fellow players and Portugal's supporters.He added: "I owe an apology to my national team teammates for having left the camp... I apologise to the Portuguese people once again, but a broken word has, for me, a defining impact."

schema.headline: Cristiano Ronaldo: Portugal forward not retiring but says he wants to be punished for walking out

title: UK risks being 'uninvestable' if new oil and gas fields not approved, warns Equinor
description: Rising energy prices have prompted renewed debate over the UK's energy security, with UK production forecast to halve by 2035.The UK already relies on
body: Rising energy prices have prompted renewed debate over the UK's energy security, with UK production forecast to halve by 2035.The UK already relies on Norway for half of its gas needs, and the Norwegian government has continued to issue new licences for oil and gas exploration in its own North Sea waters. Equinor has predicted production will remain at current levels until the middle of the next decade.Opedal said he remained confident that Prime Minister Andy Burnham's talk of a "pragmatic approach to oil and gas" meant both projects would get approved but he said the current limbo was "an uncomfortable position to be in".He said that the UK could produce more of its own oil and gas. "It's a political choice," he said. "The North Sea oil and gas industry started on the UK side. We learned from the UK and it's actually the same geology on both sides of the border - several fields actually cross it."Rosebank is the United Kingdom's largest undeveloped oil and gas field, located in the North Atlantic about 80 miles north-west of the Shetland Islands and is thought to hold up to 500 million barrels of oil and gas. Opedal told the BBC the exploration licence for the site was originally granted 25 years ago. "The licence was awarded in 2001, the discovery was made in 2004 and the final investment decision in 2023," he said.Both Rosebank and Jackdaw were initially given the go-ahead by the former Conservative government but were delayed by a legal ruling from a Scottish court, after environmental groups argued consent was given without fully considering the climate impact.Following a public consultation on the sites, which closed in August, the final decision now rests with Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh.Both Jackdaw and Rosebank are operated by Adura, a joint venture between Equinor and Shell. Aberdeen-based firm Ithaca also owns 20% of Rosebank.Adura has previously said that if approval comes soon, Jackdaw could start delivering gas to UK homes by this winter as the construction is "99% complete".

schema.headline: UK risks being 'uninvestable' if new oil and gas fields not approved, warns Equinor

title: Three arrested after raid on gang accused of helping migrants pretend to be gay to get asylum
description: Two people were arrested at addresses in London this morning on suspicion of fraud and immigration offences, with Home Office officers also seizing ph
body: Two people were arrested at addresses in London this morning on suspicion of fraud and immigration offences, with Home Office officers also seizing phones, jewellery and thousands of pounds in cash. A third person was arrested on suspicion of being in the country illegally.Chris Foster, a regional lead for criminal investigations at the Home Office, said the fake claims were connected to a Bangladeshi community LGBT organisation called Apanjon, which is based in Whitechapel, east London.He said asylum caseworkers had initially spotted patterns in suspicious claims, which raised concerns about the group, and that immigration officers had been investigating for several months."We've got some intelligence that they can provide fake letters and documents, and they could charge anywhere between £1,000 and £4,500," Foster said."It could be letters of support from Apanjon, it could be staged photographs, suggesting that these people are gay, it could be letters from people claiming to be in a friendship or a sexual relationship - [a] same-sex relationship - as the claimants."More than 100 asylum claims linked to the criminal network are being reviewed by the Home Office. Foster said some of the fake asylum applications would have "undoubtedly" been granted.Immigration judges have previously criticised evidence from Apanjon as unreliable or not credible and found that an applicant who claimed to have attended the group's events had submitted staged photographs.The Home Office said the group would often vouch for men who claimed asylum on the basis they were gay only after having initially been refused on political grounds. In one case, a man didn't raise his sexuality until nine years after his original claim.The group is accused of using the same tactics as those pushed by advisers exposed in the BBC's investigation earlier this year.A Home Office spokesperson said it was continuing to review asylum claims linked to that reporting, which led to two arrests in May.In the BBC report, published in April, an adviser called Tanisa Khan told an undercover reporter she could provide a "comprehensive package", including photographs at gay clubs and other supporting evidence.She was linked to a community group called Worcester LGBT, which she told the reporter they should attend in order to add to evidence for his fake claim.Men attending one of the group's events at a community centre in Beckton, east London, claimed they were not really gay. One said: "Nobody is a gay here. Not even 1% are gay. Not even 0.01% are gay."The investigation also revealed how bogus medical conditions and fake news websites were being used to bolster fraudulent asylum claims. Worcester LGBT has since closed. Its founder previously said the group did not create or support fabricated evidence in asylum claims and it was not up to the organisation to determine whether any individual was actually gay. Khan blamed communication difficulties for a "misunderstanding" and denied advising the reporter to make a false claim or offering to create fabricated evidence.Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood said "those faking persecution are beneath contempt and mock real victims who need protection"."To the gangs profiting from this disgraceful fraud: you will be prosecuted, stripped of your dirty money and shut down," she said."And to those cheating the system, your claim will be thrown out, and you will be removed from this country."A conviction for asylum fraud carries a maximum sentence of up to 10 years in prison.

schema.headline: Three arrested after raid on gang accused of helping migrants pretend to be gay to get asylum

title: Kemi Badenoch: I'd rather have another election than do a deal with Reform UK
description: Kemi Badenoch has said she would rather have another general election than do a deal with Reform UK to secure power, if no party wins the next electio
body: Kemi Badenoch has said she would rather have another general election than do a deal with Reform UK to secure power, if no party wins the next election.The Conservative Party leader told the BBC that Nigel Farage's Reform are "neck deep in scandal" and joining forces with them would "just be one problem after another".Polling suggests there would be a hung parliament at the next election, with Labour currently expected to be the largest party followed by Reform and the Tories.As the Conservative Party conference in Birmingham nears its end, Badenoch has also pledged to cut the cost of hiring 21 to 24-year-olds by halving the rate of employer national insurance (NI) contributions.Badenoch has been trying to position the Conservatives as a party that is different to the one that suffered an historic defeat in the 2024 general election.She told BBC Political Editor Chris Mason "we are going back to the authentic Conservative Party, that people knew and loved" after she published a 100-page document, called The Right Way, setting out the party's principles, external.Badenoch added "politics is volatile", as she tried to talk up the party's chances despite the polls suggesting only one-in-five voters would back them.She said: "We're in a different political world, and it is within that context that we know that we can win. I'm not saying that we would win."The current polling shows a hung parliament, no party getting an overall majority. "My prediction is that there would be another election immediately after. But we're the only credible alternative to Labour, the only ones with a plan."A scenario was put to Badenoch in which the Conservatives would be the largest party and Reform have a significant presence in a hung parliament after the next election. Asked if she would work with Reform in government, Badenoch replied: "If you want Conservative, you have to vote Conservative. I have said we'd have another election if there was no overall majority."Badenoch added she wants Reform voters to "come back" to the Conservatives, saying people in Farage's party are "neck deep in scandal, it'd just be one problem after another".She pointed to the arrest of Dan Thomas, who quit last month as Reform's leader in Wales after he was arrested on suspicion of assault and controlling or coercive behaviour. Thomas said he had "done nothing wrong".Badenoch also highlighted the case of Nathan Gill, the former leader of Reform in Wales who was sentenced to 10-and-a-half years in prison after admitting taking bribes for pro-Russia interviews and speeches.Farage has faced intense scrutiny over financial support he has received, including a £5m gift he received from a billionaire Reform donor before he became an MP. He has insisted he has done nothing wrong.Badenoch added: "I want to get this economy growing, I want to make the country richer, I want to stop the boats, we've got a plan on borders, we've got a plan on welfare, we've got a plan on defence and bringing energy costs down."That's what we're about."Privately, senior Conservatives talk of what they see as the importance of a potential 'tipping point' in support for the Conservatives and support for Reform UK.Tories hope that if they can draw level and then establish a small lead over Reform in opinion polls, they can begin to make the case that they are the only viable alternative to Labour winning the next general election, potentially then attracting more support.Badenoch has long said she wouldn't do a deal with Reform before the election, as it was a party trying to destroy the Conservatives.Prime Minister Andy Burnham said last month he was not tempted to call an early general election, arguing it would throw "the country into a backward-looking process". The next one must be held by August 2029.Farage has previously said Reform have "replaced the old fuddy-duddy existing Conservative Party".In her speech to the Conservative Party conference on Tuesday, Badenoch is expected to say growing the economy "will be the central organising principle of the next Conservative government" if her party wins power.She will contrast her approach with that of Burnham's government, accusing Labour of "reckless" spending, adding billions to the national debt and increasing taxes.Pitching the fight against Labour as "a battle for the soul of this nation", she will argue her party is "a renewed Conservative Party fighting again for the belief that what people earn belongs to them, not government".Elsewhere in her BBC interview, Badenoch said she was making changes to a policy for young people and was now proposing cutting the rate of employer National Insurance (NI) on earnings from 15% to 7.5% for those aged 21 to 24.The Tories announced last year that young people would see the first £5,000 of NI they would have paid in their first job redirected into a nominated savings account of their choice. The party said the policy, dubbed the "First Job Bonus", would have cost £2.8bn a year.On Tuesday, Badenoch said youth unemployed has "skyrocketed" and "you can't give people a first jobs bonus if they're not getting a first job".She added: "We're adapting and updating our policy so that it works for the problems they have today."The Conservatives said the new policy is targeted at starter jobs and the standard rate would apply to earnings above £50,270.They added it "smooths the cliff edge" which exists as employer NI goes from 0% to the full rate when a worker turns 21.The government has faced calls to reduce employer NI contributions for younger workers to help boost job opportunities. Around one million young people in the UK are not in education, employment or training.Asked why the Conservatives were not proposing to cut NI for everyone, Badenoch said: "We have to find the money first. "So we have a golden economic rule. We are being fiscally credible. We find savings and then we spend it. "If I could afford to cut it for everybody, I promise you that I would. But young people have a much worse problem than everybody else."A Labour Party spokesperson said the NI announcement was "more fantasy economics from the Tories", adding the party had "allowed nearly one million of the next generation to be locked out of work or training".

schema.headline: Kemi Badenoch: I'd rather have another election than do a deal with Reform UK

title: Froyo's made a comeback. But at £12 a tub will it last?
description: Kiersten Paterno was one of the many people willing to queue up to an hour to treat herself to some frozen yoghurt."It was a 45-minute wait for my tur
body: Kiersten Paterno was one of the many people willing to queue up to an hour to treat herself to some frozen yoghurt."It was a 45-minute wait for my turn but the whole experience of choosing your flavours and customising it with different toppings was a big part of the appeal for me," the 19-year-old student says.Froyo was a huge trend in the UK in the late 2000s and early 2010s and was most popular in London.Chains like Snog had 10 stores in the capital at its peak and other brands like AngelBerry had shops in Bristol and Brighton.And this year it's made a comeback, driven by nostalgia, social media and its perception as a healthier dessert choice.Several brands such as Go Greek, Myka and Yo-Chi launched in London, while Frurt, which operates mainly in the north west of England and Yorkshire, has opened new stores, including one in Leicester.These companies saw hundreds of customers queueing to create their own dessert pot, despite it not being a particularly cheap treat, with tubs costing as much as £12.But how likely is the current froyo craze to survive? After all, it was huge in the 2010s but by the end of that decade was all but dead.Vhari Russell, founder of Food Marketing Experts, says: "Market over-saturation played a role in the initial disappearance of froyo, as well as the natural cycle of dying trends."Market leader Snog faced increasing competition from the likes of Yog, Yoomoo and Pinkberry, while consumers also realised that the dessert may not have been the healthier option they initially thought it was."But now 2010s throwbacks coupled with a modern twist are seeing huge appetite across the market," says Russell.Will £12 for a tub eventually start to put people off though?Russell doesn't believe so, as she calls it an "affordable luxury".Going out for a froyo can be "an experiential moment" as much as anything, she adds."For many people, they don't smoke or have expensive lifestyles, so froyo isn't viewed as food, it's viewed as an experience."

schema.headline: Froyo's made a comeback. But at £12 a tub will it last?

title: 'Asos hacked': What can I do to protect myself?
description: Image caption, The message, which Asos says people should not engage with, popped up on many Asos app users' home screens on TuesdayIf a strange-looki
body: Image caption, The message, which Asos says people should not engage with, popped up on many Asos app users' home screens on TuesdayIf a strange-looking message from Asos popped up on your phone on Tuesday, you may be worrying what it could mean and whether you need to do anything. The online retailer has emailed customers apologising for the "unauthorised push notification" containing an external link, adding that they should disregard the message and not click on it.Here's what has happened, and what those who may have been affected are being advised to do.What message did people receive?On Tuesday morning, Asos users across the UK were sent pop-up messages from its app that appear to have been sent by hackers trying to extort the company."Dear ASOS DPO and IT, we have fully compromised the Snowflake instance. Engage with us, or we will leak it," the message read.Later that day, Asos said it took immediate action to restrict the apparent hackers' access, was investigating and working with advisers and relevant authorities on "next steps".Data storage company Snowflake told the BBC its investigations had "found no compromise" of its platform.What does this mean for my data?At this stage it isn't clear what information, if any, has been accessed.On Tuesday evening, Asos told customers it may include "basic personal information including name and contact details". "However, we don't believe that any payment-card information or account passwords have been impacted," it added.While those who received the pop-up message will undoubtedly be concerned, it does not mean your phone has been hacked.What can I do to protect myself?For now, the advice is:Don't click the link: The hack notification included a link to a Telegram account - Asos and cyber security experts say not to click on itChange passwords: It's worth updating your password, including across other sites that use the same one as your Asos account. The advice for a strong password is to mix numbers, symbols and upper and lower case characters, and avoid using the same password across multiple accountsTurn on two-step verification for important apps like banking and email: The National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) calls this "one of the most effective ways to protect your online accounts from cyber criminals". You can usually turn it on by going into the security settings in your accountMonitor transactions: Keep an eye on your online transactions for anything unusualBe alert going forwardAccording to Charlotte Wilson, head of enterprise at global cyber-security firm Check Point, "the biggest immediate risk may be what happens next". She says criminals know people will be searching for information online and expects there to be "attempts to exploit that confusion". Her advice to Asos customers is not to be "scared and frightened". But she says they should be "extremely suspicious" of emails, texts or messages claiming their account has been compromised, offering a refund or asking them to click a link to reset their password.People should hang up the phone if they receive any calls from someone they think might be posing as Asos or another organisation, says Which? spokesperson Kat Cereda. The consumer rights expert says they should contact the organisation themselves afterwards through separate means.'An awful lot' we don't knowIt's been less than 24 hours since the notification popped up on people's phones, and there are a number of unanswered questions.It isn't yet clear who is behind the message, what their motivation is, how many people received the notification or how many may be impactedWilson, from the cyber-security firm Check Point, says there's still "an awful lot" we don't know. Asos said its website and app were operating "as normal, and customers can continue to shop with confidence on ASOS as normal" as of Tuesday night.It said protecting customers "is our priority", and it will provide a further update "as soon as we have confirmed more information". People should visit Asos's official website directly for updates.

schema.headline: 'Asos hacked': What can I do to protect myself?

title: 'That nagging feeling of dread': Is 'hang-xiety' a real thing?
description: Image source, Eleanor TobinImage caption, Eleanor Tobin (right) says she's no stranger to hang-xiety after a night outByChloe HaywardHealth reporterYo
body: Image source, Eleanor TobinImage caption, Eleanor Tobin (right) says she's no stranger to hang-xiety after a night outByChloe HaywardHealth reporterYou wake up. Your head throbs. Then comes the second wave: a low, gnawing horror at what you might have done.You scroll back through last night's messages, certain you said something wrong. You replay conversations worried you offended someone, embarrassed yourself, or both."It's that nagging feeling of dread," says 25-year old Eleanor Tobin who works in marketing and events in London."If the day starts with me doing a checklist of my things - panically checking I have my bag, my phone - I know the anxiety is going to seep into everything I do beyond just reliving the night before."This is hang-xiety,  a name coined in social slang a decade ago, for the anxiety that can accompany a hangover.And yes, it is real."Alcohol affects the body in many ways - the brain, sleep, hormones and nervous system - that all help explain why a night out drinking can be followed by an excessively anxious morning," says Celia Morgan, professor of psychopharmacology at the University of Exeter.Figure caption, Watch: Yes, hang-xiety is a real thingWhat alcohol does to your brainAlcohol affects two chemical messengers in the brain: GABA and glutamate.GABA acts a little like the brain's braking system, reducing nerve-cell activity. Glutamate is involved in excitation and alertness.Alcohol enhances the effects of GABA and suppresses some glutamate activity, helping to produce that familiar feeling of relaxation and lowered inhibitions.But the brain is constantly trying to restore balance. As alcohol wears off, the nervous system can swing towards greater alertness and arousal.This can trigger anxiety. "Everything is always 100% worse in my mind when you have a hangover than in reality," says Tobin.A 2023 study of over 5,000 students from the UK and the Netherlands, concluded that 18.3% reported symptoms of anxiety when hungover.Image source, Eleanor TobinImage caption, For the 25-year-old, it can lead to an anxious spiral at the end of a weekendGenes play a partStudies also suggest that not everyone gets hang-xiety, and the level of anxiety does not neatly correlate with how much you drink the night before. Existing psychological characteristics – and potentially genetics – appear to play a part.In 2019 researchers at the University of Exeter studied this in 97 social drinkers. Those who drank reported a spike in anxiety the following day compared with a control group who stayed sober. The effect was strongest in people who had scored highly for shyness before drinking.Morgan's research found that shy drinkers often felt less anxious during the evening itself. Alcohol was doing exactly what they hoped, quieting social nerves, but the rebound came the next day."Shy people were hit even harder the next morning, with hugely elevated anxiety markers, especially when compared with those that weren't naturally shy," says Morgan.Hormonal and psychological chaosThere is a psychological layer, too.Innocuous moments get reinterpreted as embarrassing. A perfectly normal joke becomes, in the retelling inside your own head, a terrible mistake.The anxious spiral can outlast the physical symptoms, because it feeds on itself: worry disrupts thinking, and disrupted thinking produces more worry.If Tobin has been out Friday and Saturday night, by Sunday that spiral can become overwhelming."Suddenly taking the underground can feel like a challenge - normal stuff feels hard when you got a really bad case of the 'Sunday scaries' triggered by two hangovers in a row," she says.Image source, David Cheskin/PA WireImage caption, Drinking alcohol can affect sleep as well as trigger severe anxiety the next dayYou may have fallen asleep quickly after drinking, but that doesn't mean you've had a good night's sleep, researchers warn.Alcohol disrupts sleep, including the pattern of rapid eye movement (REM) sleep, which is important for emotional regulation. Wake up dehydrated and sleep-deprived, and your ability to cope with anxious thoughts is already reduced."Light and broken sleep means you wake feeling on edge," says Dr Alanna Hare, President of the British Sleep Society. "Even if you have eight hours in bed, you haven't had a proper night's sleep, and a tired brain is more reactive to worry."What actually helpsThe advice from researchers is unglamorous but consistent. Moderating alcohol intake matters more than any remedy taken afterwards. Drinking water between alcoholic drinks can help, so can eating during your night out. UK guidelines recommend no more than 14 units a week, the equivalent to six pints of beer or six medium glasses of wine, spread across several days.Alcohol Change UK director Andrew Misell says it's important not to reach for alcohol to manage or mask stress."Alcohol turns into a depressant and can exacerbate all sorts of problems with our physical and mental health," he says, advising people to see their GP if they are struggling with the spiral. Talking to a close friend can also be a good starting point. And perhaps the most useful trick if you are suffering with hang-xiety is to reframe the thoughts. Recognising hang-xiety as a temporary state, rather than proof that something has gone horribly wrong socially, can blunt its power.The dread is real. The catastrophe it points to usually isn't.So the next time the Sunday morning spiral sets in, remember it may simply be your brain and body trying to regain balance after alcohol.

schema.headline: 'That nagging feeling of dread': Is 'hang-xiety' a real thing?
